topic: Operating practice, emergencies, Volunteer Monitors and HF operation (G2B, G2D; 22 pool questions)

notes.front: What is priority access to a frequency?
notes.back: The right to use a frequency ahead of others; under the rules, no amateur station has it except during emergencies.
notes.explanation: This keeps the band a shared, first-come resource except when lives or safety are at stake.
notes.example: A regular net does not get to bump another contact off frequency just because the net always meets there.

notes.front: What is a station in distress?
notes.back: A station signalling it needs urgent help, which you should acknowledge and assist if you hear it.
notes.explanation: Recognising this call quickly is the first step to helping, so operators are taught to react immediately.
notes.example: Hearing an unfamiliar station break into your contact reporting a medical emergency.

notes.front: What is the Volunteer Monitor Program?
notes.back: A program of amateur volunteers formally enlisted to monitor the airwaves for rule violations and encourage self-regulation.
notes.explanation: It uses trained amateur volunteers to monitor the airwaves.
notes.example: A Volunteer Monitor comparing beam headings with colleagues to locate a station holding a repeater open.

notes.front: What is an azimuthal projection map?
notes.back: A map centred on a chosen location that shows true bearings and distances from that point.
notes.explanation: It is the tool amateurs use to aim directional antennas correctly toward distant stations.
notes.example: Centring the map on your own station shows you exactly which compass heading points at a station in Japan.

notes.front: What is the short path to a distant station?
notes.back: The more direct of the two great-circle routes between two points on Earth.
notes.explanation: Signals usually travel this way, but sometimes the longer route is actually stronger.
notes.example: Pointing a beam due east for a station that is roughly east of you is using the short path.

notes.front: What is the long path to a distant station?
notes.back: The great-circle route 180 degrees opposite the short-path heading, going the “long way round”.
notes.explanation: Ionospheric conditions can sometimes favour this longer route over the direct one.
notes.example: Pointing a beam west, instead of east, to reach a station that is normally worked by pointing east.

notes.front: What is the NATO phonetic alphabet?
notes.back: A standard set of words, Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta and so on, used to spell letters clearly over voice.
notes.explanation: It avoids the confusion of similar-sounding letters like “M” and “N”.
notes.example: Spelling a call sign as “Kilo Echo One Alpha Bravo Charlie” instead of just the raw letters.

notes.front: Why do many amateurs keep a station log?
notes.back: To help answer a request from the FCC about the station's operation.
notes.explanation: A log is not required by rule for most operation, but it is useful evidence if ever questioned.
notes.example: Recording each contact's date, time, frequency and call sign in a logbook or logging program.

notes.front: What is QRP operation?
notes.back: Deliberately transmitting at low power.
notes.explanation: Operators use it as a challenge or to reduce equipment size and power needs.
notes.example: Making a contact using only 5 W output instead of a full-power transmitter.

notes.front: When is the general “no priority access” rule set aside?
notes.back: During emergencies.
notes.explanation: 97.101(c): "At all times and on all frequencies, each control operator must give priority to stations providing emergency communications."

notes.front: What should you do first if a station in distress breaks into your contact?
notes.back: Acknowledge the station in distress and determine what assistance may be needed.
notes.explanation: Finding out what help is needed comes before any other reaction, such as ceasing transmission entirely.

notes.front: What is good practice if propagation changes and creates interference during a contact?
notes.back: Try to resolve the interference with the other stations in a mutually acceptable manner.
notes.explanation: No station has an automatic claim to the frequency, so cooperation is the expected approach.

notes.front: What minimum frequency separation should you use when selecting a CW transmitting frequency?
notes.back: 150 Hz to 500 Hz.
notes.explanation: Narrower separation risks interfering with an adjacent CW signal.

notes.front: What minimum frequency separation should you use when selecting an SSB transmitting frequency?
notes.back: 2 kHz to 3 kHz.
notes.explanation: SSB's wider bandwidth needs more separation than CW to avoid overlap.

notes.front: How can you check a frequency is clear before calling CQ?
notes.back: Send “QRL?” on CW, or ask if the frequency is in use on phone, then give your call sign.
notes.explanation: This checks for an existing contact you might not be able to hear both sides of.

notes.front: What practice complies with commonly accepted amateur convention when choosing a calling frequency?
notes.back: Following the voluntary band plan.
notes.explanation: The band plan is voluntary, not a Part 97 rule, but ignoring it causes avoidable friction.

notes.front: What is the voluntary restriction on 50.1–50.125 MHz for stations in the 48 contiguous states?
notes.back: Only contacts with stations not within the 48 contiguous states.
notes.explanation: This DX window keeps that narrow segment open for long-distance contacts.

notes.front: Who may be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES?
notes.back: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license.
notes.explanation: 97.407(a) also requires civil-defense enrolment, but holding the FCC licence is the baseline test the pool keys on.

notes.front: How often may RACES training drills be conducted without special authorization?
notes.back: No more than 1 hour per week.
notes.explanation: With state approval, drills may run up to 72 hours, but only twice a year.

notes.front: What is good practice for net management regarding frequencies?
notes.back: Have a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions.
notes.explanation: A backup avoids losing the net entirely if the primary frequency becomes unusable.

notes.front: What is an objective of the Volunteer Monitor Program?
notes.back: To encourage amateur radio operators to self-regulate and comply with the rules.
notes.explanation: The program aims at voluntary compliance, not licensing or emergency communications, which are separate functions.

notes.front: How may Volunteer Monitors localize a station holding a repeater on with a continuous carrier?
notes.back: By comparing beam headings on the repeater input from their home locations with those of other Volunteer Monitors.
notes.explanation: Triangulating multiple directional bearings pinpoints the source station's location.

notes.front: What is the recommended way to call CQ on HF looking for any contact?
notes.back: Repeat “CQ” a few times, then “this is” and your call sign a few times, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary.
notes.explanation: The listening pause is essential, since a call with no pause gives no one the chance to answer.

notes.front: What identification is required when participating in an HF contest?
notes.back: Identify your station according to normal FCC regulations.
notes.explanation: Contest rules do not relax or change the ordinary station identification rules.

notes.front: Why are signal reports typically exchanged at the start of an HF contact?
notes.back: To allow each station to operate according to conditions.
notes.explanation: Knowing how well you are being heard lets both operators adjust their approach for the contact.

notes.front: Which of the following is true concerning access to frequencies?
notes.back: Except during emergencies, no amateur station has priority access to any frequency
notes.choices:
A) Nets have priority
B) QSOs in progress have priority
C) Except during emergencies, no amateur station has priority access to any frequency
D) Contest operations should yield to non-contest use of frequencies
notes.choicesExplained: A: nets get no special priority under the rule. B: an ongoing QSO gets no special priority under the rule. D: no such yielding requirement exists in the rule.
notes.explanation: 97.101(b),(c) gives no station priority access except in emergencies.

notes.front: What is the first thing you should do if you are communicating with another amateur station and hear a station in distress break in?
notes.back: Acknowledge the station in distress and determine what assistance may be needed
notes.choices:
A) Inform your local emergency coordinator
B) Acknowledge the station in distress and determine what assistance may be needed
C) Immediately decrease power to avoid interfering with the station in distress
D) Immediately cease all transmissions
notes.choicesExplained: A: notifying a coordinator is a later step, not the first action. C: decreasing power does not address the distress call. D: stopping transmission entirely does not help assess what is needed.
notes.explanation: Acknowledging and assessing the need comes before any other step.

notes.front: What is good amateur practice if propagation changes during a contact creating interference from other stations using the frequency?
notes.back: Attempt to resolve the interference problem with the other stations in a mutually acceptable manner
notes.choices:
A) Advise the interfering stations that you are on the frequency and that you have priority
B) Decrease power and continue to transmit
C) Attempt to resolve the interference problem with the other stations in a mutually acceptable manner
D) Switch to the opposite sideband
notes.choicesExplained: A: no station has priority to claim. B: decreasing power does not resolve the shared-frequency problem. D: switching sideband does not address interference from co-channel use.
notes.explanation: No station has priority, so cooperative resolution is the expected approach.

notes.front: When selecting a CW transmitting frequency, what minimum separation from other stations should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
notes.back: 150 Hz to 500 Hz
notes.choices:
A) 5 Hz to 50 Hz
B) 150 Hz to 500 Hz
C) 1 kHz to 3 kHz
D) 3 kHz to 6 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: too narrow for practical separation. C: that range is closer to the SSB separation, not CW. D: too wide; unnecessary for a narrow CW signal.
notes.explanation: 150–500 Hz matches CW's narrow bandwidth.

notes.front: When selecting an SSB transmitting frequency, what minimum separation should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
notes.back: 2 kHz to 3 kHz
notes.choices:
A) 5 Hz to 50 Hz
B) 150 Hz to 500 Hz
C) 2 kHz to 3 kHz
D) Approximately 6 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: far too narrow for an SSB signal. B: that range is the CW separation, not SSB. D: wider than necessary for SSB separation.
notes.explanation: 2–3 kHz matches SSB's wider occupied bandwidth.

notes.front: How can you avoid harmful interference on an apparently clear frequency before calling CQ on CW or phone?
notes.back: Send “QRL?” on CW, followed by your call sign; or, if using phone, ask if the frequency is in use, followed by your call sign
notes.choices:
A) Send “QRL?” on CW, followed by your call sign; or, if using phone, ask if the frequency is in use, followed by your call sign
B) Listen for 2 minutes before calling CQ
C) Send the letter “V” in Morse code several times and listen for a response, or say “test” several times and listen for a response
D) Send “QSY” on CW or if using phone, announce “the frequency is in use,” then give your call sign and listen for a response
notes.choicesExplained: B: a fixed 2-minute listen is not the specified method. C: sending “V” or “test” is not the accepted check. D: announcing “QSY” or that the frequency is in use is not the accepted check for a clear frequency.
notes.explanation: Sending QRL? or asking if the frequency is in use, then identifying, is the accepted check.

notes.front: Which of the following complies with commonly accepted amateur practice when choosing a frequency on which to initiate a call?
notes.back: Follow the voluntary band plan
notes.choices:
A) Listen on the frequency for at least two minutes to be sure it is clear
B) Identify your station by transmitting your call sign at least 3 times
C) Follow the voluntary band plan
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: no fixed two-minute listening period is specified. B: no rule requires identifying three times before initiating a call. D: only C reflects accepted practice here.
notes.explanation: Following the voluntary band plan is the accepted practice; the other options are not specified requirements.

notes.front: What is the voluntary band plan restriction for US stations transmitting within the 48 contiguous states in the 50.1 MHz to 50.125 MHz band segment?
notes.back: Only contacts with stations not within the 48 contiguous states
notes.choices:
A) Only contacts with stations not within the 48 contiguous states
B) Only contacts with other stations within the 48 contiguous states
C) Only digital contacts
D) Only SSTV contacts
notes.choicesExplained: B: the window is for contacts outside, not within, the 48 states. C: the restriction is not mode-specific to digital. D: the restriction is not mode-specific to SSTV.
notes.explanation: This segment is voluntarily reserved as a DX window for contacts outside the lower 48.

notes.front: Who may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES to assist relief operations during a disaster?
notes.back: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license
notes.choices:
A) Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license
B) Only a RACES net control operator
C) A person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license or an appropriate government official
D) Any control operator when normal communication systems are operational
notes.choicesExplained: B: being a net control operator alone is not the rule's requirement. C: a government official without an amateur licence does not qualify. D: 97.407(a) requires an FCC licence and civil-defence enrolment, whatever the state of normal communications.
notes.explanation: 97.407(a) requires an FCC-issued amateur licence, alongside civil-defense enrolment.

notes.front: Which of the following is good amateur practice for net management?
notes.back: Have a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions
notes.choices:
A) Always use multiple sets of phonetics during check-in
B) Have a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions
C) Transmit the full net roster at the beginning of every session
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: multiple phonetic sets are not a required practice. C: reading the full roster every session is not required. D: only B reflects accepted good practice here.
notes.explanation: A backup frequency is standard good practice; the other options are not required.

notes.front: How often may RACES training drills and tests be routinely conducted without special authorization?
notes.back: No more than 1 hour per week
notes.choices:
A) No more than 1 hour per month
B) No more than 2 hours per month
C) No more than 1 hour per week
D) No more than 2 hours per week
notes.choicesExplained: A: too long an interval; the rule sets a weekly, not monthly, cap. B: too long an interval; the rule sets a weekly, not monthly, cap. D: too long; the rule caps routine drills at 1 hour, not 2.
notes.explanation: 97.407(d)(4) caps routine drills at 1 hour per week.

notes.front: What is the Volunteer Monitor Program?
notes.back: Amateur volunteers who are formally enlisted to monitor the airwaves for rules violations
notes.choices:
A) Amateur volunteers who are formally enlisted to monitor the airwaves for rules violations
B) Amateur volunteers who conduct amateur licensing examinations
C) Amateur volunteers who conduct frequency coordination for amateur VHF repeaters
D) Amateur volunteers who use their station equipment to help civil defense organizations in times of emergency
notes.choicesExplained: B: that describes Volunteer Examiners, a separate program. C: that describes frequency coordinators, a separate role. D: that describes RACES/ARES operators, a separate role.
notes.explanation: The program is specifically about monitoring for rule violations, not exams, coordination or civil defense.

notes.front: Which of the following are objectives of the Volunteer Monitor Program?
notes.back: To encourage amateur radio operators to self-regulate and comply with the rules
notes.choices:
A) To conduct efficient and orderly amateur licensing examinations
B) To provide emergency and public safety communications
C) To coordinate repeaters for efficient and orderly spectrum usage
D) To encourage amateur radio operators to self-regulate and comply with the rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: licensing exams are the VE program's role, not the Volunteer Monitor Program's. B: emergency communications are a separate function. C: repeater coordination is a separate function.
notes.explanation: Encouraging self-regulation and compliance is the program's stated objective.

notes.front: What procedure may be used by Volunteer Monitors to localize a station whose continuous carrier is holding a repeater on in their area?
notes.back: Compare beam headings on the repeater input from their home locations with that of other Volunteer Monitors
notes.choices:
A) Compare vertical and horizontal signal strengths on the input frequency
B) Compare beam headings on the repeater input from their home locations with that of other Volunteer Monitors
C) Compare signal strengths between the input and output of the repeater
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: comparing polarizations is not the described method. C: comparing input/output strength does not localize the source. D: only B is the described localization method.
notes.explanation: Comparing directional beam headings from multiple monitors lets them triangulate the source.

notes.front: Which of the following describes an azimuthal projection map?
notes.back: A map that shows true bearings and distances from a specific location
notes.choices:
A) A map that shows accurate land masses
B) A map that shows true bearings and distances from a specific location
C) A map that shows the angle at which an amateur satellite crosses the equator
D) A map that shows the number of degrees longitude that an amateur satellite appears to move westward at the equator with each orbit
notes.choicesExplained: A: accurate land-mass shape is not its defining feature, and it distorts shape away from the centre. C: satellite crossing angle is a different concept. D: satellite orbital drift is a different concept.
notes.explanation: It is centred on a location and shows true bearings and distances from that point.

notes.front: Which of the following indicates that you are looking for an HF contact with any station?
notes.back: Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” then your call sign a few times, then pause to listen, repeat as necessary
notes.choices:
A) Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call” -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
B) Say “QTC” followed by “this is” and your call sign -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
C) Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” then your call sign a few times, then pause to listen, repeat as necessary
D) Transmit an unmodulated carried for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen -- repeat as necessary
notes.choicesExplained: A: signing once without “CQ” is not the standard general-call method. B: “QTC” signals traffic to send, not a general call. D: an unmodulated carrier is not the standard general-call method.
notes.explanation: This is the standard HF general call structure, ending with a listening pause.

notes.front: How is a directional antenna pointed when making a “long-path” contact with another station?
notes.back: 180 degrees from the station’s short-path heading
notes.choices:
A) Toward the rising sun
B) Along the gray line
C) 180 degrees from the station’s short-path heading
D) Toward the north
notes.choicesExplained: A: sunrise direction is unrelated to long path by definition. B: gray-line alignment is a separate propagation concept. D: long path is defined relative to the short-path heading, not a fixed compass direction.
notes.explanation: Long path is defined as the opposite great-circle direction from the short path.

notes.front: Which of the following are examples of the NATO Phonetic Alphabet?
notes.back: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta
notes.choices:
A) Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog
B) Adam, Boy, Charles, David
C) America, Boston, Canada, Denmark
D) Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta
notes.choicesExplained: A: an older, non-NATO phonetic set. B: not a recognised phonetic alphabet. C: not a recognised phonetic alphabet.
notes.explanation: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta are the standard NATO phonetics.

notes.front: Why do many amateurs keep a station log?
notes.back: To help with a reply if the FCC requests information about your station
notes.choices:
A) The FCC requires a log of all international contacts
B) The FCC requires a log of all international third-party traffic
C) The log provides evidence of operation needed to renew a license without retest
D) To help with a reply if the FCC requests information about your station
notes.choicesExplained: A: no such blanket FCC logging requirement exists. B: no such blanket FCC logging requirement exists. C: licence renewal does not require a log as evidence.
notes.explanation: A log is useful evidence if the FCC asks about the station, though not generally required by rule.

notes.front: Which of the following is required when participating in a contest on HF frequencies?
notes.back: Identify your station according to normal FCC regulations
notes.choices:
A) Submit a log to the contest sponsor
B) Send a QSL card to the stations worked, or QSL via Logbook of The World
C) Identify your station according to normal FCC regulations
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: submitting a log to the sponsor is contest custom, not an FCC requirement. B: sending QSLs is a custom, not an FCC requirement. D: only C is an actual FCC requirement.
notes.explanation: Only the ordinary FCC identification requirement is a rule requirement; the others are contest customs.

notes.front: What is QRP operation?
notes.back: Low-power transmit operation
notes.choices:
A) Remote piloted model control
B) Low-power transmit operation
C) Transmission using Quick Response Protocol
D) Traffic relay procedure net operation
notes.choicesExplained: A: unrelated to model aircraft control. C: not a real protocol name. D: not related to traffic-relay nets.
notes.explanation: QRP denotes deliberately low-power operation.

notes.front: Why are signal reports typically exchanged at the beginning of an HF contact?
notes.back: To allow each station to operate according to conditions
notes.choices:
A) To allow each station to operate according to conditions
B) To be sure the contact will count for award programs
C) To follow standard radiogram structure
D) To allow each station to calibrate their frequency display
notes.choicesExplained: B: award-program eligibility is not the reason reports are exchanged. C: radiogram structure is unrelated to a routine HF signal report. D: signal reports do not calibrate a frequency display.
notes.explanation: Knowing signal conditions lets each operator adjust power, speed or mode as needed.

notes.front: How do short path and long path differ?
notes.back: Short path is the direct great-circle route; long path is 180 degrees opposite, the longer way round.
notes.explanation: Which one carries the stronger signal depends on ionospheric conditions along each route at that moment.

notes.front: How does the recommended minimum frequency separation differ for CW and SSB?
notes.back: CW: 150–500 Hz. SSB: 2–3 kHz.
notes.explanation: SSB occupies far more bandwidth than CW, so it needs much more room from the next signal.
